Identify if the missingness has a pattern.

An Upset-plot is generated to identify if the missingness of value has a pattern. We observe that the missing values for vehicle values and fuel_type are likely independent. Whereas vehicle and age are missing together but there are only 2 rows affected by it. If we are using vehicle values and fuel_type Missing at Random seems to be in play here

Code 
gg_miss_upset(df, nsets = 4)

# 1. Run your categorical transformation for fuel_type (Mapping NA to "Unknown")
df_clean <- df %>%
  mutate(
    fuel_type = case_when(
      fuel_type == 'D' ~ "Diesel",
      fuel_type == 'G' ~ "Gasoline",
      is.na(fuel_type) ~ "Unknown", # Label the 36% missing values explicitly
      TRUE             ~ "Others"
    ),
    fuel_type = factor(fuel_type, levels = c("Gasoline", "Diesel", "Unknown", "Others"))
  )

# 2. Build the Bar Chart Layer (p1)
p1 <- ggplot(data = df_clean, aes(x = fuel_type, fill = fuel_type)) +
  geom_bar(color = "grey25", alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Frequency Distribution of Fuel Types",
    subtitle = "Explicitly highlighting missing data as 'Unknown'",
    x = "Fuel Type Classification", 
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Fuel Type"
  )

# 3. Build the Numerical Missingness Audit Data Frame
missing_audit_data <- df %>%
  summarise(
    `Total Missing Rows` = format(sum(is.na(fuel_type)), big.mark = ","),
    `Missing Percentage` = paste0(round(mean(is.na(fuel_type)) * 100, 2), "%")
  )

# 4. Turn the data frame into a graphical table layer (p2)
p2 <- ggtexttable(missing_audit_data, rows = NULL)

# 5. Stitch them together vertically using patchwork
p1 / p2 + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(4, 1))

Data Cleaning

Clean up of data, data type conversion and new variable creation

  • Convert all categorical values with acronym into readable label
  • Remove the 2 rows of data where vehicle age and age driving license is null
  • Impute Median to vehicle age and mode to fuel type
  • We also created indicator called underwriting profit to identify which portfolios are losses.
Code 
# Create function to calculate mode
calc_mode <- function(x) {
  distinct_values <- unique(x[!is.na(x)])
  distinct_values[which.max(tabulate(match(x, distinct_values)))]
}

# Pre-calculate the mode safely outside the pipeline to unblock the compiler
fuel_mode <- calc_mode(df$fuel_type)

df_transformed <- df %>%
  mutate(
    # All the factor like variables
    policy_type = case_when(
      policy_type == "TP"     ~ "Basic Third-Party",
      policy_type == "TPG"    ~ "Third-Party with Glass Cov",
      policy_type == "CC"     ~ "Third-Party with two or more Cov",
      policy_type == "COMP_E" ~ "Comprehensive with Excess",
      policy_type == "COMP_N" ~ "Comprehensive without Excess",
      TRUE                    ~ "Others"
    ),
    policy_status = case_when(
      policy_status == 'A' ~ "Active",
      policy_status == 'C' ~ "Cancelled",
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    business_type = case_when(
      business_type == 'NB' ~ "New_Business",
      business_type == 'P' ~ "Portfolio",
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    payment_frequency = case_when(
      payment_frequency == 'A' ~ "Annual",
      payment_frequency == 'S' ~ "Semi-Annual",
      payment_frequency == 'Q' ~ "Quarterly",
      TRUE                     ~ "Others"
    ),
    bonus_score = case_when(
      bonus_score == 'G' ~ "Positive",
      bonus_score == 'N' ~ "Neutral",
      bonus_score == 'B' ~ "Negative",
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    fuel_type = case_when(
      fuel_type == 'D' ~ "Diesel",
      fuel_type == 'G' ~ "Gasoline",
      is.na(fuel_type) ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    municipality_type = case_when(
      municipality_type == 'I' ~ "Inland",
      municipality_type == 'C' ~ "Coastal",
      municipality_type == 'IS' ~ "Islands",
      TRUE                     ~ "Others"
    ),
    circulation_area = case_when(
      circulation_area == 'U' ~ "Urban",
      circulation_area == 'R' ~ "Rural",
      TRUE                    ~ "Others"
    ),

    # These are all the numeric conversions
    vehicle_value = as.numeric(vehicle_value),
    power_to_weight_ratio = as.numeric(power_to_weight_ratio),
    total_premium = as.numeric(total_premium),
    liability_premium = as.numeric(liability_premium),
    property_damage_premium = as.numeric(property_damage_premium),
    theft_premium = as.numeric(theft_premium),
    fire_premium = as.numeric(fire_premium),
    glass_premium = as.numeric(glass_premium),
    legal_protection_premium = as.numeric(legal_protection_premium),
    occupants_premium = as.numeric(occupants_premium),
    total_incurred = as.numeric(total_incurred),
    liability_incurred = as.numeric(liability_incurred),
    liability_property_incurred = as.numeric(liability_property_incurred),
    liability_injury_incurred = as.numeric(liability_injury_incurred),
    property_incurred = as.numeric(property_incurred),
    theft_incurred = as.numeric(theft_incurred),
    fire_incurred = as.numeric(fire_incurred),
    glass_incurred = as.numeric(glass_incurred),
    legal_protection_incurred = as.numeric(legal_protection_incurred),
    occupants_incurred = as.numeric(occupants_incurred),
    total_exposure = as.numeric(total_exposure),
    liability_exposure = as.numeric(liability_exposure),

    # New variables created
    underwriting_profit = total_premium - total_incurred
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    policy_type = factor(policy_type, levels = c(
      "Basic Third-Party",
      "Third-Party with Glass Cov",
      "Third-Party with two or more Cov",
      "Comprehensive with Excess",
      "Comprehensive without Excess",
      "Others"
    )),
    # Directly reference the column in median calculation to be safe
    vehicle_value = replace_na(vehicle_value, median(vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    policy_status = as.factor(policy_status),
    business_type = as.factor(business_type),
    payment_frequency = as.factor(payment_frequency),
    # Use the static pre-calculated scalar value here
    fuel_type = as.factor(replace_na(fuel_type, fuel_mode)),
    municipality_type = as.factor(municipality_type),
    circulation_area = as.factor(circulation_area),
    bonus_score = as.factor(bonus_score)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(vehicle_age))

For columns imputed check distribution before and after

Code 
# 2. Re-create your comparative dataset (Long format)
df_before <- df %>%
  select(vehicle_value) %>%
  mutate(vehicle_value = as.numeric(vehicle_value), status = "Before")

df_after <- df_transformed %>%
  select(vehicle_value) %>%
  mutate(status = "After")

df_compare <- bind_rows(df_before, df_after) %>% filter(!is.na(vehicle_value))

# 2. Generate the side-by-side comparative violin plot safely
p1 <- ggplot(df_compare, aes(x = "Vehicle Value Profile", y = vehicle_value, fill = status)) +
  # Layer 1: Draw Left Half (Before Imputation)
  see::geom_violinhalf(
    data = filter(df_compare, status == "Before"),
    flip = FALSE, 
    alpha = 0.6, 
    color = "grey30"
  ) + 
  # Layer 2: Draw Right Half (After Imputation)
  see::geom_violinhalf(
    data = filter(df_compare, status == "After"),
    flip = TRUE,   # Only flip this specific layer
    alpha = 0.6, 
    color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Before" = "#f8766d", "After" = "#00bfc4")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Imputation Audit: Vehicle Value Distribution",
    subtitle = "Comparing raw data density against median-imputed data",
    x = "", 
    y = "Vehicle Value ($)",
    fill = "Status"
  )

summary_table_data <- df_compare %>%
  group_by(status) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Rows = comma(n()),
    Mean_Value = comma(mean(vehicle_value), accuracy = 1),
    Median_Val = comma(median(vehicle_value), accuracy = 1),
    Std_Dev    = comma(sd(vehicle_value), accuracy = 1)
  ) %>%
  rename(Status = status, `Total Rows` = Total_Rows, `Mean ($)` = Mean_Value, `Median ($)` = Median_Val, `SD ($)` = Std_Dev)

# 4. Create the Graphic Table Layer (p2)
p2 <- ggtexttable(summary_table_data, rows = NULL)

# 5. Use Patchwork to stitch them vertically and set heights
# The plot takes 80% of the vertical space, the table takes 20%
p1 / p2 + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(4, 1))

1. Financial health of the business

  • Chart A
    • We want to display the overall premiums earned and claims paid out to understand the trending and year on year change for each year.
  • Chart B
    • We want to show percentage change in net profitability from year to year taking into account this years profit - previous year profit / absolute of previous year profit
  • Chart C
    • We wish to understand for each unit of exposure, how much dollar are we expecting, is the trade off increasing or decreasing
Code 
yearly_summary <- df_transformed %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(
    sum_premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum_incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    underwriting_profit = sum_premium - sum_incurred,
    avg_rev_per_exposure = sum_premium / sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  # Calculate YoY changes
  mutate(
    premium_yoy = (sum_premium - lag(sum_premium)) / lag(sum_premium) * 100,
    incurred_yoy = (sum_incurred - lag(sum_incurred)) / lag(sum_incurred) * 100
  )

# =========================================================================
# STEP 2: Pivot & Format Labels for Plot 1 (Grouped Bars)
# =========================================================================
p1_data <- yearly_summary %>%
  select(year, `Total Premium` = sum_premium, `Total Incurred Claims` = sum_incurred, premium_yoy, incurred_yoy) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Total Premium`, `Total Incurred Claims`), 
    names_to = "Metric", 
    values_to = "Amount"
  ) %>%
  # Assign the correct YoY percentage to the correct metric row
  mutate(
    yoy_val = if_else(Metric == "Total Premium", premium_yoy, incurred_yoy),
    # Format text: If it's the first year, just show amount. Otherwise, show amount + YoY %
    label_text = case_when(
      is.na(yoy_val) ~ label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale(), prefix = "$")(Amount),
      yoy_val >= 0   ~ paste0(label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale(), prefix = "$")(Amount), "\n(+", round(yoy_val, 1), "%)"),
      TRUE           ~ paste0(label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale(), prefix = "$")(Amount), "\n(", round(yoy_val, 1), "%)")
    )
  )

# =========================================================================
# STEP 3: Build Plot 1 - Grouped Bar Chart with Value & % Labels
# =========================================================================
# Explicitly defining bar positioning width so the text alignments align flawlessly
bar_width <- 0.6
dodge_width <- 0.7

p1 <- ggplot(p1_data, aes(x = factor(year), y = Amount, fill = Metric)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = dodge_width), width = bar_width) +
  
  # Add dynamic text labels on top of bars
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label_text),
    position = position_dodge(width = dodge_width),
    vjust = -0.25,       # Pushes text slightly above the bar boundary
    size = 3,            # Clean font size to prevent overlapping
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 0.85    # Cleans up spacing between the raw amount and the % text line
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Total Premium" = "#2ca02c", "Total Incurred Claims" = "#d9534f")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale(), prefix = "$"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)) # Adds 15% headroom at the top so labels don't clip
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "A: Premium Inflow vs. Claims Outflow",
    x = NULL, 
    y = "Total Financial Amount (Y-O-Y % Increase)", 
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# =========================================================================
# STEP 4: Build Plot 2 - Net Underwriting Profit Trend with Labels
# =========================================================================
yearly_summary <- yearly_summary %>%
  mutate(
    profit_label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale(), prefix = "$")(underwriting_profit)
  )

p2 <- ggplot(yearly_summary, aes(x = factor(year), y = underwriting_profit, fill = underwriting_profit > 0)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = profit_label, vjust = if_else(underwriting_profit >= 0, -0.4, 1.4)),
    size = 3,

  ) +
  labs(

  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(

3. Premiums from 2022 to 2024

  • This is to perform confirmatory data analysis that there is a change in distribution amongst the various product over the years

Where Null Hypothesis: The distribution of total premium is identical across all three years Alternative Hypothesis: The distribution of total premium is not identical across all three years; at least one year’s premium distribution stochastically dominates

  • We also observed that there are extreme values in total premiums, hence a log is applied to the y axis to help observe the full range of premiums more easily

Create function

Code 
plot_policy_distribution <- function(data, target_policy, target_metric = "total_premium") {
  
  # 1. Dynamically filter and prepare data based on function arguments
  # We use .data[[target_metric]] to allow passing the column name as a string
  plot_data <- data %>%
    filter(
      policy_type == target_policy,
      .data[[target_metric]] > 0
    ) %>%
    mutate(year = factor(year))
  
  # Determine dynamic text for labels
  metric_label <- gsub("_", " ", target_metric) %>% tools::toTitleCase()
  
  # 2. Safe Statistical Check
  unique_years <- unique(plot_data$year)
  
  if (length(unique_years) > 1) {
    # Dynamically build formula: target_metric ~ year
    formula_obj <- as.formula(paste(target_metric, "~ year"))
    stat_test   <- kruskal.test(formula_obj, data = plot_data)
    
    stat_label  <- paste0(
      "Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = ", round(stat_test$statistic, 2),
      ", df = ", stat_test$parameter,
      ", p-value = ", scales::scientific(stat_test$p.value, digits = 3)
    )
  } else if (length(unique_years) == 1) {
    stat_label <- paste0("Kruskal-Wallis: Insufficient groups (Only ", unique_years, " data available)")
  } else {
    # If string matching yields 0 rows, print warning and stop to avoid ggplot crash
    warning(paste0("No data found for policy type: '", target_policy, "' with ", metric_label, " > 0."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 3. Generate the Plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = .data[[target_metric]], fill = year)) +
    
    # The Half-Eye distribution view
    stat_halfeye(
      adjust = 0.5,
      width = 0.6,
      .width = c(0.66, 0.95),
      point_color = "black",
      interval_color = "black",
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    
    # Scale and formatting
    scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(prefix = "$")) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", guide = "none") +
    
    # Informative labels that update dynamically based on your inputs
    labs(
      title = paste0(metric_label, " Distribution across Years"),
      subtitle = paste0(target_policy, "\n", stat_label),
      x = "Year",
      y = paste0(metric_label, " (Log Scale)")
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", size = 10, face = "italic"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    ) +
  coord_flip() 
  return(p)
}


plot_pairwise_matrix <- function(data, target_policy, target_metric = "total_premium") {
  
  # 1. Filter data based on input arguments
  plot_data <- data %>%
    filter(
      policy_type == target_policy,
      .data[[target_metric]] > 0
    ) %>%
    mutate(year = factor(year))
  
  # Clean up the metric name for beautiful axis/title labels
  metric_label <- gsub("_", " ", target_metric) %>% tools::toTitleCase()
  
  # 2. Check if pairwise testing is mathematically possible
  if (length(unique(plot_data$year)) < 2) {
    warning(paste0("Skipping matrix: '", target_policy, "' does not have enough distinct years with data."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 3. Execute the Pairwise Wilcoxon Test with Holm Adjustment
  wt_result <- pairwise.wilcox.test(
    x = plot_data[[target_metric]], 
    g = plot_data$year,
    p.adjust.method = "holm"
  )
  
  p_matrix <- wt_result$p.value
  
  # Handle edge case where the matrix is completely empty/NULL
  if (all(is.na(p_matrix))) {
    warning(paste0("No valid variance found to compute pairwise shifts for '", target_policy, "'."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 4. Transform matrix to a tidy long-format dataframe
  p_df_long <- as.data.frame(p_matrix) %>%
    mutate(Group_B = rownames(.)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -Group_B, 
      names_to = "Group_A", 
      values_to = "p_val"
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(p_val)) %>%
    mutate(
      # Ensure factor matching for explicit manual scale mapping
      is_significant = factor(p_val < 0.05, levels = c("TRUE", "FALSE")),
      p_label = if_else(p_val < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste0("p = ", round(p_val, 3)))
    )
  
  # 5. Build the Dynamic Matrix Plot
  p <- ggplot(p_df_long, aes(x = Group_A, y = Group_B, fill = is_significant)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = p_label), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
    
    # Red/Coral for significant shifts, neutral grey for stagnant periods
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c("TRUE" = "#2ca02c", "FALSE" = "#7f8c8d"),
      labels = c("TRUE" = "Significant Shift (p < 0.05)", "FALSE" = "No Stat. Difference"),
      name = "Holm Conclusion",
      drop = FALSE 
    ) + 
    
    # FORCE the legend preview boxes to show their true assigned colors manually
    guides(
      fill = guide_legend(
        override.aes = list(fill = c("#2ca02c", "#7f8c8d"))
      )
    ) + 
    
    labs(
      title = paste0("Pairwise Post-Hoc Shifts Matrix (", metric_label, ")"),
      subtitle = paste0(target_policy, "\nWilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Holm-Adjusted Method)"),
      x = "Baseline Year (Group A)",
      y = "Comparison Year (Group B)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", face = "italic", size = 10, margin = margin(b = 10)),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
  
  return(p)
}

Observation from Customer Plans

⚠️Third-Party with two or more Cov:

  • Total Premium Distribution change is associated with more lower priced premiums, although the median remain relatively similar.

  • Median of claims stayed the same from 2022 to 2024 but the number of $1000 (log scale) claims increases sharply. There are also more variation of claims below the 25th percentile of all claims

⚠️Comprehensive with Excess:

  • Distribution change seems to be associated with more lower priced premiums, although the medium remain relatively similar.

  • Overall distribution is statistically significant (p = 2.23e-03) when using the Kruskal Wallis Test, but shows a statistically insignificance when using the Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test with Holm Adjusted method. This shows that on a year on year basis, there is no big change in the claims and its stable but a change is observable from 2022 and 2024. The claims is stable and predictable

✅Comprehensive without excess: - Pricing for this category seems to have move to a higher tier as compared to 2023 and 2022 as more motor insurance plans has shifted to a higher premium tier.

  • General shape of the claims are rather similar amongst the 3 years, and similarly to our claims, there are two distinct peaks in the distribution.

  • claim and pricing display similar patterns and no drastic movement is observed

✅Third Party with Glass Cov - Although this is change in distribution when comparing the 3 years. The year 2022 and 2024 (\(p-value = 0.043\)) is very close to the alpha value tolerance level of 0.05. This could mean that the distribution is nearing the distribution from 2024 to 2022.

  • Claims stayed relative stable and predictable.

⚠️Basic Third Party Plan:

  • The Interquartile range of this price plan shortern and differs from 2022 and 2023. We also observed a split peak for the distribution for 2024 meaning there could be another sub group in this product. It is also likely the case that the 2024 total premiums has remain the same as 2022 as per the (\(p-value = 0.062\))

  • Claim pattern have change as well from the bulge in claims around the medium claims in 2024 as compared to 2022 and 2023. IQR now is longer and less predictable.

                  labels = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-45", "46-55", "56-65", "66+")),
    v_age_bin = cut(vehicle_age, 
                    breaks = c(-1, 3, 6, 10, 15, Inf), 
                    labels = c("0-3 yrs", "4-6 yrs", "7-10 yrs", "11-15 yrs", "16+ yrs"))
  ) %>%
  # Group by the bins to isolate each intersection pocket
  group_by(age_bin, v_age_bin) %>%
  # Calculate aggregate metrics per cell
  summarise(
    total_policies = n(),
    total_liability_claims = sum(liability_property_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    # Calculate the Claim Rate (Frequency per policy/exposure)
    claim_rate = total_liability_claims / total_policies,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Optional: Filter out empty or extremely low-volume cells to remove noise
  filter(total_policies > 10)

# 2. Plot the binned matrix
ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = v_age_bin, y = age_bin, fill = claim_rate)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", lwd = 0.5, linetype = 1) +
  # Use a color scale that makes high values (the spike) pop out vividly
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1, name = "Claim Rate") +
  # Add the actual text values inside the tiles for quick confirmation
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(claim_rate, accuracy = 0.1)), 
            color = "white", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "Liability Claim Frequency Matrix",
    subtitle = "Identifying localized risk spikes across driver and vehicle age pockets",
    x = "Vehicle Age Group",
    y = "Driver Age Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

Code 
 corr_data <- df_transformed %>%
  select(
    driver_age, 
    vehicle_age,

    power_to_weight_ratio,
    liability_property_claims  # Your target claim count metric
  ) %>%
  # Ensure all selected features are strictly evaluated as numeric matrices
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%

# 2. Generate the statistical correlation matrix
ggcorrmat(
  data = corr_data,
  type = "spearman",          # Use "nonparametric" for Spearman or "bayesian" if preferred
  colors = c("#2c7bb6", "#ffffbf", "#d7191c"), # Classic blue-to-red diverging scale
  title = "Portfolio Risk Profile: Correlation Matrix Matrix",
  subtitle = "Evaluating linear relationships across driver metrics, vehicle assets, and claim outcomes",
  show.legend = TRUE,
  matrix.type = "upper",        # Shows top triangle to remove visual redundancy
  lab.size = 3.5,               # Size of correlation coefficients inside the squares
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)
Code 
# 1. Isolate and clean the factors
cramer_df <- df_transformed %>%
  filter(policy_type == "Basic Third-Party") %>%
  select(
    policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, 
    bonus_score, fuel_type, vehicle_brand, 
    municipality_type, circulation_area
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.factor))

# 2. Compute the exact 8x8 Cramér's V matrix mathematically
cat_vars <- colnames(cramer_df)
n_vars <- length(cat_vars)
v_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_vars, ncol = n_vars, dimnames = list(cat_vars, cat_vars))

for (i in 1:n_vars) {
  for (j in 1:n_vars) {
    # Generate cross-tabulation table
    contingency_table <- table(cramer_df[[cat_vars[i]]], cramer_df[[cat_vars[j]]])
    # Store the scalar Cramer's V value
    v_matrix[i, j] <- assocstats(contingency_table)$cramer
  }
}

# 3. Convert the matrix to a long data frame format for ggplot
v_long <- as.data.frame(v_matrix) %>%
  mutate(Variable1 = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -Variable1, names_to = "Variable2", values_to = "CramersV")

# 4. Plot a clean, beautifully spaced association tile grid
ggplot(v_long, aes(x = Variable1, y = Variable2, fill = CramersV)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#ffffbf", mid = "#fdae61", high = "#d7191c", 
                       midpoint = 0.5, limit = c(0, 1), name = "Cramér's V") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(CramersV, 2)), color = "black", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Clean Categorical Feature Association Matrix",
    subtitle = "Calculated via global chi-square contingencies | Exactly 8x8 Dimensions",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

Code 
## driver age
premium_exposure_analysis <- df_transformed %>%
  filter(policy_type == "Third-Party with two or more Cov") %>%
  mutate(
    age_bin = cut(driver_age, 
                  breaks = c(17, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, Inf), 
                  labels = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-45", "46-55", "56-65", "66+"))) %>%
  group_by(age_bin) %>%
  summarise(
    total_premium  = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_exposure = sum(liability_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(total_exposure > 0) %>%
  mutate(avg_premium_per_exposure = total_premium / total_exposure)

# 1. Rename the variable to match its true mathematical scope
plan_avg_premium <- sum(premium_exposure_analysis$total_premium) / sum(premium_exposure_analysis$total_exposure)

# 2. Update the conditional logic flag
premium_exposure_analysis <- premium_exposure_analysis %>%
  mutate(
    pricing_status = ifelse(
      avg_premium_per_exposure >= plan_avg_premium, 
      "Above/At Plan Average", 
      "Below Plan Average"
    )
  )

# 3. Update the ggplot layers to use the correct labels
p1 <- ggplot(premium_exposure_analysis, aes(x = age_bin, y = avg_premium_per_exposure, fill = pricing_status)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = "white", lwd = 0.5) +
  
  # Update the threshold line target
  geom_hline(yintercept = plan_avg_premium, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Update the text label mapping onto the chart space
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = plan_avg_premium + 15, 
           label = paste0("    Plan Average Baseline: $", round(plan_avg_premium, 2)), 
           color = "gray30", fontface = "italic", size = 3.5) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Above/At Plan Average" = "#2ca02c", "Below Plan Average" = "#d62728")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Premium Revenue per Unit of Exposure Year",
    subtitle = "Slicing Third-Party with two or more Cov plan to spot sub-group underpricing",
    x = "Driver Age Group",
    y = "Premium Revenue / Exposure Year ($)"
  )

  mutate(avg_premium_per_exposure = total_premium / total_exposure)

# 1. Rename the variable to match its true mathematical scope
plan_avg_premium <- sum(premium_exposure_analysis$total_premium) / sum(premium_exposure_analysis$total_exposure)

# 2. Update the conditional logic flag
premium_exposure_analysis <- premium_exposure_analysis %>%
  mutate(
    pricing_status = ifelse(
      avg_premium_per_exposure >= plan_avg_premium, 
      "Above/At Plan Average", 
      "Below Plan Average"
    )
  )

# 3. Update the ggplot layers to use the correct labels
p2 <-ggplot(premium_exposure_analysis, aes(x = v_age_bin, y = avg_premium_per_exposure, fill = pricing_status)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = "white", lwd = 0.5) +
  
  # Update the threshold line target
  geom_hline(yintercept = plan_avg_premium, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Update the text label mapping onto the chart space
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = plan_avg_premium + 15, 
           label = paste0("    Plan Average Baseline: $", round(plan_avg_premium, 2)), 
           color = "gray30", fontface = "italic", size = 3.5) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Above/At Plan Average" = "#2ca02c", "Below Plan Average" = "#d62728")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Premium Revenue per Unit of Exposure Year",
    subtitle = "Slicing Third-Party with two or more Cov plan to spot sub-group underpricing",
    x = "Vehicle Age Group",
    y = "Premium Revenue / Exposure Year ($)"
  )


p1 + p2
